summary: Learners build the habit of asking 'is this answer sensible?' by using rounding/estimation as an INDEPENDENT check on a calculation, and by judging the level of accuracy a context actually needs. Two intertwined ideas: (1) an estimate sets a ballpark that can disprove an exact answer in seconds (if 47,832 + 23,156 is about 71,000, an answer of 3,988 must be wrong), and (2) the right precision depends on purpose (a stadium crowd is honestly '52,000'; a shop bill must be exact). The two ideas are one habit, not separate tricks, and the check is deliberately NOT a re-computation of the same sum.
misconceptions: Thinks a good estimate should EQUAL the exact answer (so treats the small difference as an error)
Checks by recomputing exactly rather than estimating - defeating the purpose
Believes more accuracy is always better; cannot see when rounding is appropriate
Rounds to an unhelpful level (too coarse to discriminate, or too fine to be an estimate)
Treats the estimate itself as the required answer

activities.title: The estimate as a lie-detector: prove an answer wrong without redoing it
steps: Take a completed sum with its answer, e.g. 47,832 + 23,156 = 3,988.
Round each number to a useful grain (nearest 1,000: about 48,000 and about 23,000) WITHOUT recomputing the exact sum.
Add the rounded numbers to get a ballpark of about 71,000.
State whether the given answer is possible: 3,988 is nowhere near 71,000, so it must be wrong - perhaps a place-value, alignment or copying slip; the estimate shows that it is wrong, not why.
Decide, for a stated context, whether a nearest-100 or a nearest-1,000 estimate is the better grain, and justify which keeps enough discrimination to be a useful check.
Repeat with other answers, including one that is close to the estimate (e.g. 70,988) and judge whether 'close' is enough to trust.
Explain, in your own words, why this check catches the error faster than redoing the full algorithm.
activities.insight: An estimate is an independent order-of-magnitude check: it can PROVE an answer impossible in seconds without ever doing the exact calculation. An estimate is a deliberate ballpark, not a rival exact answer.

activities.title: Honest precision: choosing the right level of accuracy for the purpose
steps: Consider a context, e.g. a newspaper reporting a football crowd. Decide whether it should print '52,000' or '51,847', and say why.
Argue that a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly while '51,847' implies a false precision nobody actually counted.
Contrast with a shop totting up a customer's bill: decide whether 'about 52 pounds' is acceptable and explain why money (and any count that must balance) needs exactness.
Rank several context cards (crowd / money / distance / stock count) by how much precision each honestly needs, giving a reason for each.
Identify a case where rounding a crowd to '50,000' would be TOO rough - when might that coarse figure hide something that matters?
activities.insight: The right level of accuracy is a decision with reasons tied to purpose and audience - not 'more digits is always better'. Spurious precision can be misleading; appropriate rounding can be more honest.

activities.title: Convince the sceptic (spoken reasoning)
steps: In role with a sceptical editor/partner, justify out loud why a proposed answer must be impossible, using only an estimate.
Argue, when challenged, why '52,000' is the honest figure to print for a crowd and why a bill demands exact pounds and pence.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Could an answer be close to your estimate and still be wrong?' and 'How close is close enough to trust?'
Explain how the estimate check and the accuracy choice are the same underlying habit - asking whether a number is sensible for its purpose.
activities.insight: Judging reasonableness and defending a level of accuracy is reasoning you can articulate and defend, not just a computed value; the two moves are one habit, not separate tricks.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the impossible answer and sort by needed precision
steps: Given an estimate, select which of several proposed answers is impossible (e.g. an answer near 4,000 when the estimate is about 71,000).
Sort contexts into 'needs an exact figure' vs 'a rounded figure is honest'.
For each choice, briefly state the reason rather than only choosing the option.
activities.insight: Recognising impossible answers and matching precision to context are checkable skills; adding a short reason connects them to the underlying judgement.

checkQuestion: A pupil works out 47,832 + 23,156 and writes 3,988. Without doing the exact sum yourself, how could you tell straight away that this answer must be wrong? Then a different question: if a newspaper reports the crowd at a football match, should it print '52,000' or '51,847' - and why? Talk me through your thinking on both.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning rounds each number (about 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000), so any answer near 4,000 is impossible - it is an order of magnitude out, probably a place-value or alignment slip - and this is spotted WITHOUT the exact sum. On accuracy: a crowd figure is inherently approximate, so '52,000' communicates the scale honestly and '51,847' implies a false precision nobody counted; but for money, or counts that must balance, exactness is the point. The right level of accuracy depends on the PURPOSE, not on having more digits.
